content: The Hospital Incident Command System (HICS) is a comprehensive framework designed to manage incidents in both emergency and non-emergency situations. It equips hospitals of all sizes with the necessary tools to enhance their emergency preparedness and response capabilities, both as individual entities and as part of the broader response community. HICS is derived from the Hospital Emergency Incident Command System (HEICS), which was developed in the late 1980s to provide a foundational structure for the more than 6,000 hospitals in the United States to prepare for and respond to various types of disasters. During the development of the fourth edition of HEICS, it became evident that an incident management system could also be valuable for daily operations, pre-planned events, and non-emergency situations. As a result, HICS was created to address both emergent and non-emergent scenarios, such as relocating hospital facilities, distributing medications to staff, or planning for large-scale hospital or community events. The development of HICS was led by a National Work Group consisting of 20 hospital subject-matter experts from across the United States. Additionally, ex officio members were included to ensure alignment with governmental, industrial, and hospital accreditation planning efforts and requirements. The principles of the Incident Command System (ICS) are designed to achieve several objectives: Establish a clear chain of command to manage all routine or planned events, regardless of size or type. Integrate personnel from different agencies or departments into a unified structure capable of addressing issues and delegating responsibilities effectively. Provide logistical and administrative support to operational personnel as needed. Ensure that key functions are covered while avoiding duplication of efforts. The incident planning process is implemented regardless of the size or complexity of the incident. This includes assigning appropriate resources to complete tasks, monitoring their performance, and making necessary adjustments, such as reallocating resources or modifying tactics. The Homeland Security Presidential Directive-5 (HSPD-5), issued by President George W. Bush in February 2003, established the National Incident Management System (NIMS). Before NIMS, there was no standardized framework for domestic incident response that unified all levels of government and emergency response agencies. NIMS provides a structure for interoperability and compatibility among various members of the response community. It creates a flexible framework that enables governmental and non-governmental agencies to collaborate effectively at all levels during all phases of an incident, regardless of its size, complexity, or location. The Emergency Operations Plan (EOP) outlines a hospital’s strategy for responding to and recovering from realized threats, hazards, or other incidents. This document provides overall direction and coordination for the hospital’s response structure and processes. An effective EOP lays the foundation for implementing the Incident Command System and ensures the necessary communication and coordination between operating groups. The process of developing an effective emergency management program includes the following steps: Appointing an Emergency Program Manager. Establishing an Emergency Management Committee. Developing an all-hazards Emergency Operations Plan. Conducting a Hazard Vulnerability Analysis. Creating incident-specific guidance (Incident Planning Guides). Coordinating with external entities. Training key staff members. Exercising the EOP and incident-specific guidance through a structured exercise program. Reviewing and evaluating the program. Learning from identified lessons to promote organizational improvement. The HICS incident management team charts illustrate the hospital command functions, showing how authority and responsibility are distributed within the incident management team. Activities at the Hospital Command Center (HCC) are directed by the Incident Commander, who holds overall responsibility for all operations within the HCC. The Incident Commander may appoint additional Command Staff personnel to assist as needed. Many incidents are likely to involve injured or ill patients. The Operations Section is tasked with managing the tactical objectives outlined by the Incident Commander. This section includes branches such as Department Level, Patient Care, Infrastructure, Business Continuity, Security, and Hazardous Materials (HazMat). The Planning Section is responsible for collecting, evaluating, and disseminating incident situation information and intelligence to the Incident Command. It includes units such as the Resources Unit, Situation Unit, Documentation Unit, and Demobilization Unit. The Logistics Section coordinates support requirements, while the Finance/Administration Section manages the costs associated with the response. Additional incident command principles and practices are also addressed, including staff identification, building depth within the incident command team, job action sheets, and incident response guides.
